22566-dorothy-and-the-wizard-in-oz:
Dorothy and the Wizard in Oz brings two old friends back together. L. Frank Baum's readers had asked for more about the Wizard. Children wrote to him asking what happened to the Wizard afterward.

The Wizard had made hosts of friends in the first Oz book. He frankly acknowledged himself a humbug in that story. Yet children loved him and remembered his balloon ascent. They were all waiting for him to come down again someday. So Baum tells what happened to the Wizard afterward in this volume. Dorothy joins him underground after an earthquake opens the earth. Their adventures run through strange countries beneath the surface. Readers get a favorite pair reunited in Oz's fourth book.
24459-the-lost-princess-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum published this Oz book in Chicago in 1917, with pictures by John R. Neill. It was the eleventh book of the Oz series. When Ozma, the lovely girl ruler of Oz, vanishes, her friends set out to find her.

Dorothy and her companions travel across Oz, meeting old friends and strange new creatures, while the search leads toward the thief who stole Ozma's magic. Baum's tale keeps the series' mix of humour, invention, and gentle adventure. Young readers get another trip across Oz, with its talking animals, odd kingdoms, and loyal friendships.
25519-little-wizard-stories-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum offers six short Oz tales for young readers, illustrated by John R. Neill. The Cowardly Lion meets the Hungry Tiger, Dorothy and Toto have a small adventure of their own, and Tik-Tok faces the Nome King in separate, self-contained stories.

Ozma and the Little Wizard, Jack Pumpkinhead with the Sawhorse, and the Scarecrow beside the Tin Woodman complete the set. Each story stays short and gentle, giving children a single Oz friendship or scrape to enjoy without needing the longer Oz novels. A child can enjoy one tale at a sitting, then return for the next.
25581-rinkitink-in-oz:
L. Frank Baum writes this 1916 Oz novel, illustrated by John R. Neill and published in Chicago by Reilly and Britton. Baum dedicates it to his new grandson, Robert Alison Baum, and introduces a boy hero readers had never met before.

Dorothy returns among the girls in the story, and the cast strays far from Oz before gathering in the Emerald City for Ozma's feast. Baum promises a tale quite different from other Oz histories, with Rinkitink, a jolly king figure, at its comic centre. Inga travels with Rinkitink and his talking goat Bilbil.
26624-the-road-to-oz:
L. Frank Baum published this Oz book with Reilly and Britton at Chicago in 1909, with pictures by John R. Neill. Baum says children deluged him with letters begging for more Dorothy, so he returned to Oz despite plans to write other stories. Toto is back, and new friends join Dorothy on the road, including the Shaggy Man, Button-Bright, and Polychrome, the Rainbow's Daughter.

The road runs through a queer village, the city of beasts, and the Scoodlers, with an escape from a soup-kettle and a crossing of the Deadly Desert. Tik-Tok, Billina, and Jack Pumpkinhead appear before the Emerald City and Princess Ozma's birthday celebration. Baum dedicates the book to his first grandson, Joslyn Stanton Baum, and writes only to please children.
30537-the-royal-book-of-oz:
The Royal Book of Oz, copyrighted in 1921, continues L. Frank Baum's Oz stories in a volume enlarged and edited by Ruth Plumly Thompson and illustrated by John R. Neill. In it, the Scarecrow traces his ancestry and learns he rules the Silver Island as its long-lost emperor.

Dorothy and the Cowardly Lion rescue him and bring him back to Oz. Publishers explain that Baum left unfinished notes on Princess Ozma, Dorothy, and the jolly people of Oz, and promised to shape them into a new book. Thompson, who knew and loved the Oz stories, carries that promise forward in a bright, child-friendly sequel.
32094-the-patchwork-girl-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum's The Patchwork Girl of Oz, published in Chicago by Reilly and Lee in 1913 with drawings by John R. Neill, follows his earlier Oz books: The Road to Oz, Dorothy and the Wizard in Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, The Land of Oz, and Ozma of Oz. Baum dedicated the book to Sumner Hamilton Britton of Chicago. Its prologue explains Baum's curious position as Royal Historian of Oz.

Through the kindness of Dorothy Gale of Kansas, afterward Princess Dorothy of Oz, Baum says he was once appointed Royal Historian, with the privilege of chronicling that fairyland. After six books, however, Ozma of Oz decreed that her country would thereafter be invisible to outsiders, and all communication would be cut off. Children who loved the Oz stories were as sorry as their historian. Readers get another Oz chronicle, framed by that farewell and its puzzle.
419-the-magic-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum sends Dorothy, Trot, and the Wizard on a birthday quest in this Oz tale. Their goal is a magical gift for Princess Ozma, but two rogues, Kiki and Ruggedo, plot to seize Oz with a stolen magic word. Beasts of the Forest of Gugu, a lonesome duck, and a glass cat join the tangle.

Baum writes in his warm, plain style, with new creatures at every turn and a party at the end. The Wizard's tricks, the lost black bag, and the fountain of oblivion keep the plot moving. Young readers will find the familiar Oz mix: peril softened by humor, and friends who save the day together.
420-dorothy-and-the-wizard-in-oz:
L. Frank Baum drops Dorothy, the Wizard, Zeb, Eureka the kitten, and Jim the cab-horse into an underground world in this Oz tale. An earthquake opens the ground beneath them, and they wander glass cities, a vegetable kingdom, and the den of wooden gargoyles. Invisible bears, dragonettes, and a trial of Eureka add peril and jest.

Baum writes with his usual warmth, letting Dorothy's kind sense steer the party home. Ozma's magic belt at last lifts them to the Emerald City. The book delights young readers with strange lands, odd folk, and a party of friends who face each wonder side by side.
485-the-road-to-oz:
L. Frank Baum sends Dorothy, the Shaggy Man, Button Bright, and Polychrome the Rainbow's Daughter down an enchanted road to Oz in this tale. They meet King Dox, a city of beasts, scoodlers with soup kettles, and Johnny Dooit, who fixes all with his tools. The deadly desert and the truth pond test them before the Emerald City.

Baum writes for children who begged for more Dorothy, and he thanks them in his preface. A grand banquet and birthday party close the road. The book delights with odd folk, kind humor, and the familiar Oz promise: friends found on the way matter more than the road's end.
517-the-emerald-city-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum brings Dorothy's aunt and uncle to live in Oz in this tale, while the Nome King plots revenge. Uncle Henry's debts threaten the Kansas farm, so Ozma grants Dorothy's wish to bring her kin to the Emerald City. Meanwhile Guph gathers whimsies, growleywogs, and phanfasms for an invasion.

Baum writes with his usual warmth, sending Dorothy through Utensia, Bunbury, and Bunnybury on a winding road home. Glinda's spell and the forbidden fountain turn the invaders back. The book, meant by Baum as an Oz farewell, delights with odd lands and the promise that home can be found anew.
54-the-marvelous-land-of-oz:
Letters from children asked L. Frank Baum for more of the Scarecrow and Tin Woodman. The Marvelous Land of Oz answers with a new hero, the boy Tip, raised by the witch Mombi. Tip flees with a pumpkin-headed companion he brings to life.

Tip and Jack Pumpkinhead reach the Emerald City as General Jinjur's army revolts. The Scarecrow and Tin Woodman return to set matters right. Magic powder, a flying sofa-bed, and a change of rulers follow. The sequel keeps Oz playful while widening its cast. Baum's Oz books continued from here, building a series that outlived its first readers.
55-the-wonderful-wizard-of-oz:
A Kansas cyclone lifts Dorothy and her dog Toto to a strange land. L. Frank Baum's Wonderful Wizard of Oz sends her down a yellow brick road to the Emerald City. She seeks the Wizard who might send her home.

On the road she frees the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion. Each wants what he thinks he lacks: brains, heart, and courage. The Wicked Witch of the West stands in their path. Baum's tale became America's best-loved fairy story. Stage and film versions followed quickly, turning Dorothy's road into a shared cultural landmark.
955-the-patchwork-girl-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz tale about Scraps, the Patchwork Girl, a lively creature stitched from many cloths and brought to life by magic. Dorothy Gale of Kansas, now Princess Dorothy of Oz, helps tell the tale, for Baum, as Royal Historian of Oz, sets down the chronicle with her kind aid.

Scraps, with her button eyes and gay patches, joins Dorothy and friends on a quest through Oz, meeting odd folk and facing the usual Oz perils with wit. Baum's humour and invention are at their brightest here. The book, dedicated to Sumner Hamilton Britton, delights young readers who love Oz at its most playful.
956-tik-tok-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz tale about Tik-Tok, the clockwork man who thinks, speaks, and acts by machinery, wound up to go. Baum dedicated the book to Louis F. Gottschalk, whose melodies breathe the true spirit of fairyland, and he tells his readers that the Oz stories please them best of all his books.

Tik-Tok joins Dorothy and friends on a quest through Oz, where his steady ticking and literal mind bring humour and help in turn. Baum's fancy runs free, with new lands and old friends. The book delights young readers who love Oz machines and magic together, and who cheer for a hero who never tires.
957-the-scarecrow-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz tale in which the Scarecrow, the straw man of Oz, sets out on a new adventure. Baum dedicated the book to the uplifters of Los Angeles, big men with generous hearts, in thanks for their kindness and good fellowship. Their spirit, he says, matches the Scarecrow's own.

The Scarecrow meets new friends and foes, crosses strange lands, and uses his brains, such as they are, to solve perils with humour. Baum's Oz wit and warmth carry the tale, with the Scarecrow's modesty at its heart. The book charms Oz fans young and old, as a tale of friendship and cleverness over force.
959-the-lost-princess-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz tale about a lost princess, dedicated to his granddaughter Ozma Baum. Baum tells his readers that youthful imagination has led mankind from the Dark Ages to the present. It led Columbus to America and Franklin to his discoveries, and he praises the imaginations his young readers show.

The tale follows Dorothy and friends as they search Oz for the missing princess, with magic, mistaken identities, and Oz humour along the way. Baum's invention stays bright, and the search ends in reunion and joy. The book delights Oz readers, as a quest that celebrates imagination itself as the greatest magic.
britannica-1911-furfooz: Furfooz is a Belgian village in the Ardennes, some ten miles from Dinant, where three caves holding prehistoric remains were dug in 1872. In the most famous, the Trou de Frontal, excavators found human skeletons with short, broad skulls, animal bones with reindeer especially plentiful, and an oval pottery vase. The Furfooz type of man is placed at the close of the Quaternary age, though Mortillet dates it to the Neolithic period.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvarez-caril:
Gil de Albornoz, renowned cardinal, general, and statesman, was born about 1310 at Cuenca in New Castile and died 23 August 1367 at Bonriposo Castle near Viterbo. His father descended from Alfonso V of León, his mother Teresa de Luna from Aragon's royal house. After law at Toulouse he became royal almoner, Archdeacon of Calatrava, and Archbishop of Toledo on 13 May 1338. He accompanied Alfonso XI against the Moors in 1340 and saved the king's life.

Sent to Italy by Innocent VI, he again subjected the whole pontifical territory to papal authority. His successor at Avignon, the Abbot of Cluny, had no military training to face the skilled Ordelaffi, and intrigues complicated the work. He remained only a short time at Avignon before returning to Italy's wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-badajoz:
Badajoz, Latin Pacensis, takes a name once thought to mark Rome's Pax Julia or Pax Augusta. That Roman Pax is now known to be Beja in Portugal, and Badajoz itself bears an Arabic name. Its bishopric rose in 1225, just after Alfonso IX of Leon reconquered the land from the Moors. Its first bishop was Don Pedro Perez, named by Alfonso X the Wise, and succession has run unbroken since.

The diocese, suffragan to Seville, holds 136 parishes in 13 vicariates, with about half a million souls. Its cathedral chapter counts five prelates, thirteen canons, and sixteen beneficed clerics, besides chaplains. A diocesan seminary trains priests, and colleges at Badajoz and Zafra serve the city and district. Leon and Castile named the region Extremadura, land beyond the Douro, and Cortes, conqueror of Mexico, was born at Medellin within it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-le-coz:
Claude Le Coz, a French bishop, was born at Plouevez-Parzay in Finistere in 1740 and died at Villevieux in the Jura in 1813. Pupil, then professor, then Quimper college principal, he took the oath in 1791. Elected schismatic Bishop of Ille-et-Vilaine, he defended his election, declared null by the pope. In the Assembly he defended Catholic colleges, church dress, and Christian marriage.

His moderation brought the Convention's severity on him; fourteen months in Mont-Saint-Michel prison followed. Under the Directory his opposition to replacing Sunday with the decadi nearly caused his deportation. Under the Concordat the Holy See took him in among the oath-taking bishops, and he became Archbishop of Besancon. Doubt lingered over whether he had retracted, since Bernier had softened its terms and Le Coz denied it. Only a weeping private interview with Pius the Seventh closed the awkwardness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hector-berlio:
French composer Hector Berlioz, born near Grenoble in 1803, abandoned medicine for the Conservatoire library and became the founder of programme music, the school that tells definite ideas and events in sound. His father sent him to Paris medical school, but harmony lessons soon produced a Mass at St. Roch, and admission to the Conservatoire in 1823 brought rebellion against Cherubini's classicism.

The Fantastic Symphony and the Prix de Rome cantata Death of Sardanapalus launched his new manner. Huge works followed: a Requiem for double chorus, vast orchestra, four military bands, and organ, and a Te Deum of equal scale. The Damnation of Faust sends Faust to perdition rather than saving him in Goethe's pantheist fashion. Liturgical texts drew him always, yet his music speaks every human passion in a fiercely subjective voice.
dorothy-and-the-wizard-in-oz:
L Frank Baum sends Dorothy Gale underground in Dorothy and the Wizard in Oz, the fourth Oz book, subtitled a faithful record of adventures in an underground world. An earthquake drops Dorothy, her cousin Zeb Hugson, the kitten Eureka, and the cab-horse Jim into a crack in the earth. The Wizard of Oz soon falls in beside them, balloon and all.

Their road home runs through a glass city, a vegetable kingdom whose people want to bury them, invisible bears, wooden gargoyles, and dragonettes. Ozma rescues the party with the magic belt, and Eureka stands trial in Oz for eating a piglet. Baum's invention stays generous, and the underground journey gives the series one of its strangest settings.
nasa-tm-19700033121-performance-of-a-10-:
Fred W. Steffen of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in October 1970. It gives the performance of a conical plug nozzle fitted with a stowed thrust reverser. Tests covered flight speeds from a standstill to twice the speed of sound.

Nozzles with two throat areas and two shroud lengths were tested. Steffen compares them with a hinged iris plug nozzle that had no reverser. With its shroud pulled back, the reverser nozzle did better at subsonic cruise, he reports. At other settings the trade went the other way. A stowed reverser lets a jet slow down after landing without harming cruise flight.
the-emerald-city-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum's The Emerald City of Oz brings Dorothy back to Oz for good. Its contents tell the arc in heads: how the Nome King grew angry, how Ozma granted Dorothy's request, and how Dorothy became a princess. The Nome King plots revenge and hires strange allies, from the Whimsies to the Growleywogs, while Dorothy tours odd lands.

Aunt Em and Uncle Henry come to live in Oz at last. Glinda's spell and a drink at the Forbidden Fountain end the threat. Baum meant this as the series' close, and it glows with a fond farewell.
the-lost-princess-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum dedicated The Lost Princess of Oz to his granddaughter Ozma Baum and opened it with a letter to his readers about imagination. Imagination, he argues, carried mankind through the Dark Ages, led Columbus and Franklin to their discoveries, and gave the world the steam engine, telephone, and automobile. A prominent educator, he says, calls fairy tales of untold value in developing that faculty in the young.

Baum then credits the book's main idea to a visitor. A sweet little girl of eleven told him that if Ozma ever got lost or stolen, everybody in Oz would be dreadful sorry. The chapter list begins with A Terrible Loss, the troubles of Glinda the Good, a robbery, and a search party, turning the child's suggestion into an Oz adventure.
the-magic-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum's The Magic of Oz bills itself, in its subtitle, as a record of the adventures of Dorothy, Trot, and the Wizard of Oz. The Cowardly Lion, the Hungry Tiger, and Cap'n Bill join them. Their quest is a magical birthday present for Princess Ozma. The twenty-three chapters promise Mount Munch, conspirators, and the Forest of Gugu. They add an isle of a magic flower, a magic word learned by the Wizard, and a lonesome duck. Ozma's birthday party and the Fountain of Oblivion close the tale.

Baum's letter to his readers begins with a bow to the world. The events of recent years outside, he says, are so marvelous that he despairs of matching them with any tale of Oz. The letter breaks ground for a tale in which the Wizard's magic becomes the prize everyone is chasing.
the-marvelous-land-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote The Marvelous Land of Oz after children flooded him with letters asking for more about the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman. In his author's note, dated from Chicago in June 1904, Baum explains that he promised one young visitor a sequel once a thousand letters arrived. The chapters introduce Tip, who builds a pumpkin-headed man and brings him alive with a magic powder.

Tip's creation, Jack Pumpkinhead, rides a sawhorse that also springs to life. The fugitives flee to the Emerald City, where the Scarecrow now rules as king. General Jinjur leads an army of revolt against him, and the party travels on to seek the Tin Woodman's help. Baum dedicated the book to the two stage actors whose Scarecrow and Tin Woodman had delighted child audiences. Young readers get invention, escape, and a comic revolution in Oz.
the-patchwork-girl-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote The Patchwork Girl of Oz, dedicated to his young friend Sumner Hamilton Britton of Chicago. The prologue explains how more Oz stories came to be written. Baum, as Royal Historian of Oz, had made six books when Ozma's edict cut the land off, invisible to the outside world, and children wrote asking for more.

A child suggested wireless telegraphy. The Historian rigged a tower, learned the art, and called for Princess Dorothy. Glinda the Sorceress, whose great book records every event the moment it happens, would be sure to notice. A Shaggy Man in Oz knew how to reply. The prologue frames the tale as messages from a hidden land.
the-road-to-oz:
L. Frank Baum, royal historian of Oz, sends Dorothy Gale of Kansas onto an enchanted road with the Shaggy Man, Button Bright, and Polychrome the Rainbow's daughter. Contents promise a way to Butterfield, a queer village, King Dox, a city of beasts, a musicker, soup-kettle escapes, a truth pond, and Tik-Tok before the Emerald City and Ozma's birthday.

A letter to readers begins by granting what children asked for: another Oz book. The road structure lets Baum string new countries and creatures between Kansas and the Emerald City. Young readers get a journey built from requests, which keeps its tone obliging and episodic.
the-scarecrow-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum dedicated The Scarecrow of Oz to the uplifters of Los Angeles, California. He thanked them for kindness, consideration, and good-fellowship. A prefatory letter, headed 'Twixt You and Me, follows the dedication. Baum signs it as Royal Historian of Oz.

In that letter, an army of child readers besieged the post office, Baum jokes. Their imperious commands reached him through conquered postmen. They insisted Trot and Cap'n Bill be admitted to the Land of Oz. Trot should enjoy Dorothy, Betsy Bobbin, and Ozma there. The one-legged sailor might befriend the Tin Woodman, the Shaggy Man, and Tik-Tok. Baum says the Scarecrow's best efforts were needed to save the pair. The story leaves them happily in Ozma's palace.
the-wonderful-wizard-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz lists twenty-four chapters in its contents. Dorothy meets the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion. The party journeys to the Emerald City and the great Oz. Later chapters bring Glinda the Good Witch and the trip home. Baum dedicates the book to his wife, his good friend and comrade.

An introduction begins by placing the tale among folklore and legend. Baum presents Oz as a modern fairy tale for children. Wonder replaces the old tales' moralizing fright. Readers follow a Kansas girl through cyclones and poppy fields. The chapter list alone maps one of America's best-loved fantasy journeys.
tik-tok-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum dedicated Tik-Tok of Oz to composer Louis F. Gottschalk, whose melodies he said breathe fairyland's true spirit. His letter to readers recalls the success of The Patchwork Girl of Oz. Children, he reports, like the Oz stories best of all.

Baum introduces Ann Soforth, Queen of Oogaboo, whom Tik-Tok helped conquer the Nome King, plus Betsy Bobbin reaching Oz. He also promises a future book bringing Trot, Cap'n Bill, Button-Bright, and Ojo together, once Dorothy sends word by wireless. Readers get an Oz adventure introduced as a direct conversation with child readers.
